articles.title: LA residents find a lifeline in this free wildfire-tracking app
articles.summary: Watch Duty has shot to the top of Apple’s free App Store charts as Californian residents look to navigate catastrophic blazes devastating LA.
articles.body: Watch Duty, a nonprofit-run app that tracks wildfires with live maps and alerts, has shot to the top of Apple’s App Store charts this week as Californian residents look to navigate catastrophic blazes devastating Los Angeles. The app launched in 2021 and is now available in 22 states, providing evacuation warnings, real-time text, photo and video updates, and a map interface with flame icons to show regions where fires are blazing. Users can access information on evacuation routes, shelter locations, and firefighting efforts, alongside zooming in on the map view to see the latest updates for precise locations. It’s a one-stop shop for everything needed during a fire emergency. Watch Duty is powered by a team of around 200 volunteers, many of which are retired or active firefighters, dispatchers, or first responders. The app pulls its wildfire information from official government reports, volunteer reporters, and 911 dispatch calls which are then vetted and monitored using radio scanners, wildlife cameras, satellites, and local announcements from law enforcement and fire services. [Media: Watch Duty says that the community-bolstered network allows it to provide more real-time information than fire-tracking services like CalFire and InciWeb which rely on government alerts. The app is used by active firefighters and has become a lifeline for people across the western United States who live in areas deemed to be high-risk fire zones — Watch Duty says its active users increased to 7.2 million by December 2024 compared to 1.9 million in 2023. Californians on social media are encouraging each other to download the app in light of the ongoing LA fires raging across thousands of acres of land fueled by high winds and extremely dry conditions. As of Thursday morning, the LA Times reports that the fires have killed five people and destroyed more than 2,000 buildings, including the homes of celebrities like Paris Hilton, Billy Crystal, Adam Brody, and James Woods. [Media: Over 367,000 California households are currently without power according to PowerOutage, and at least 130,000 LA residents are now under evacuation orders. “Seconding the Watch Duty app so hard,” said one Californian on a Threads post encouraging users to download the app. “I live in Butte County, CA, (near where the Camp Fire was in 2018) and Watch Duty has been immeasurably helpful during fires like the Park Fire last summer.” [Media: Watch Duty’s vice president of operations Nick Russell says that users are drawn to the app because it’s more accessible than manually checking several sources and social media updates, and because of its network for vetting and verifying factual information. Conspiracy theories surrounding natural disasters and climate change have become a common occurrence online, with misinformation regarding weather-related events being shared by users across social media platforms. “One of the big things for us, our big theme, is quality over quantity. We’re not in a big hurry to get information that we’re going to have to go and retract later,” Russell told NBC News on Wednesday. “And so if it takes a few extra minutes to get it out there, that’s fine, but we want it to be that official info; and because we built a one-way communication platform, we don’t offer that venue for people to circulate nonsense ... And so it really puts the ball in our court for good information.” Russell also noted that Watch Duty doesn’t collect or sell user data, instead relying on premium app subscriptions and funding from private donations to stay up and running. The core features of the app that are essential for fire monitoring, safety, and evacuation, are entirely available for free. “I think it’s really important in today’s world, where so many people are trying to profit off disaster, to really understand that that’s not what Watch Duty is,” Russell said. “Watch Duty will remain free forever.”

articles.title: Calendário lunar de novembro: veja datas da Lua cheia e outras fases | G1
articles.standfirst: Novembro terá Lua nova no dia 9 e Lua cheia no dia 24, que será uma superlua, segundo a Nasa. O mês também terá ocultação de Regulus e pico da chuva de meteoros Leônidas.
articles.summary: Novembro terá Lua nova no dia 9 e Lua cheia no dia 24. A cheia será uma superlua. O mês também terá ocultação de Regulus e pico da chuva de meteoros Leônidas.
articles.body:
A Lua Cheia nasce no Cairo (Egito) em 15 de novembro de 2024. — Foto: REUTERS/Mohamed Abd El Ghany

A Lua cheia de novembro ocorre no dia 24 , às 11h53 , no horário de Brasília. Antes disso, a Lua chega ao quarto minguante no dia 1º, à Lua nova no dia 9 e ao quarto crescente no dia 17.

A cheia deste mês será também uma superlua , segundo a Nasa, a agência espacial norte-americana, já que acontecerá pouco mais de um dia antes de o satélite atingir o perigeu , ponto de sua órbita em que fica mais próximo da Terra.

Novembro ainda reserva outros fenômenos para quem gosta de acompanhar o céu. Na madrugada do dia 3, a Lua passa na frente da estrela Regulus , a mais brilhante da constelação de Leão, em parte do Brasil.

Já no dia 7, a Lua minguante e Vênus vão aparecer próximos no céu, pouco antes do amanhecer.

Veja as datas e os horários das principais fases da Lua, no horário de Brasília:

🌗 Quarto minguante (metade da Lua iluminada, com a parte clara diminuindo): 1º de novembro, às 17h28;

🌑 Lua nova (disco praticamente invisível no céu): 9 de novembro, às 4h02;

🌓 Quarto crescente (metade da Lua iluminada, mas com a parte clara aumentando): 17 de novembro, às 8h47;

🌕 Lua cheia (disco lunar totalmente iluminado para quem observa da Terra): 24 de novembro, às 11h53.

❗ Preste atenção no seu fuso, pois os horários mudam de acordo com ele. No Acre, por exemplo, a Lua cheia ocorre às 9h53; em Fernando de Noronha, às 12h53.

Já quem espera um eclipse como o eclipse lunar parcial visto no fim de agosto terá de aguardar: novembro não terá um eclipse do tipo.

O próximo eclipse lunar ocorrerá em fevereiro de 2027 , mas será penumbral e quase imperceptível a olho nu. Um eclipse parcial volta a ser visível em todo o Brasil só em janeiro de 2028 , e um total, em junho de 2029.

A Lua não produz luz própria. O brilho que vemos no céu é a luz do Sol refletida em sua superfície.

Em qualquer momento, metade da Lua está iluminada pelo Sol. O que muda ao longo do seu ciclo então é quanto dessa parte iluminada conseguimos enxergar da Terra, conforme o satélite percorre sua órbita ao redor do planeta.

Na Lua nova, a face iluminada fica voltada principalmente para o lado oposto ao da Terra, e o disco lunar praticamente não aparece no céu. Nos dias seguintes, a parte iluminada visível aumenta.

No quarto crescente , aproximadamente metade do disco que vemos está iluminada. Essa parcela continua aumentando até a Lua cheia , quando praticamente toda a face voltada para a Terra aparece iluminada.

Depois, ocorre o caminho inverso: a área iluminada visível diminui até o quarto minguante e segue encolhendo até uma nova Lua nova.

➡️ O intervalo entre duas luas novas consecutivas é chamado de lunação .

O ciclo que começa em 9 de novembro termina em 8 de dezembro e dura cerca de 29 dias e meio. Por isso, as fases da Lua não acompanham exatamente o começo e o fim dos meses do calendário.

Lua cheia é vista no início do eclipse lunar no Cairo, no Egito, nesta sexta-feira (28). — Foto: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/Reuters

A Lua cheia ocorrerá em 24 de novembro , às 11h53 , no horário de Brasília. Como isso acontece durante o dia, o melhor momento para observá-la será depois do pôr do Sol.

Em São Paulo (SP), a Lua nasce por volta das 18h57. No Rio de Janeiro (RJ), às 18h41; em Recife (PE), às 17h33; em Brasília (DF), às 18h44; e em Porto Alegre (RS), às 19h34.

A Lua cheia também será considerada uma superlua , porque ocorrerá quando o satélite estiver próximo do ponto de sua órbita em que fica mais perto da Terra.

No dia 24, a Lua estará a cerca de 361 mil quilômetros do nosso planeta. No dia seguinte, essa distância será ainda menor, de aproximadamente 359 mil quilômetros .

Essa proximidade faz com que a Lua pareça um pouco maior e mais brilhante do que em outras luas cheias.

Ao nascer, próxima ao horizonte, a Lua também poderá parecer maior devido a uma ilusão de ótica e apresentar tons amarelados ou avermelhados por causa da atmosfera.

Na madrugada de 3 de novembro, a Lua vai passar na frente de Regulus, a estrela mais brilhante da constelação de Leão, e escondê-la temporariamente.

Em São Paulo (SP), a estrela deve desaparecer atrás da Lua por volta das 4h43. Em Brasília (DF), isso ocorre às 4h32; em Belo Horizonte (MG), às 4h44; e em Curitiba (PR), às 4h41.

A Lua estará minguante , com cerca de um terço de sua superfície visível iluminada.

O fenômeno, porém, não poderá ser observado em todo o Brasil. Em cidades como Recife (PE), Fortaleza (CE) e Belém (PA), a estrela não será encoberta.

Imagem feita de Pitangueiras (SP), na região de Ribeirão Preto (SP), por câmera fotográfica de conjunção entre Lua e Vênus. — Foto: José Carlos Salerno

Na madrugada de 7 de novembro, a Lua minguante e Vênus também vão aparecer muito próximos no céu, pouco antes do amanhecer.

Para observar, será preciso olhar para o horizonte leste. A aproximação é apenas aparente, já que os dois astros continuam separados por milhões de quilômetros no espaço.

No dia 15 de novembro, Marte e Júpiter também vão aparecer próximos no céu e poderão ser observados antes do nascer do Sol.

Novembro também será marcado pela chuva de meteoros Leônidas , formada por fragmentos deixados pelo cometa 55P/Tempel-Tuttle .

O fenômeno atinge seu pico em meados do mês, e a melhor oportunidade de observação no Brasil deve ocorrer na madrugada de 18 de novembro.

Em São Paulo (SP), o período mais favorável deve começar por volta das 2h e seguir até pouco antes do amanhecer, quando a constelação de Leão estará mais alta no céu.

Para observar os meteoros, não é necessário usar telescópio ou binóculo. O ideal é procurar um local escuro, longe das luzes das cidades, e observar uma área ampla do céu.

No dia 20 de novembro, Mercúrio poderá ser observado antes do amanhecer, quando atingirá sua maior distância aparente do Sol no céu.

Já no dia 25, Urano estará em uma posição favorável para observação, permanecendo acima do horizonte durante boa parte da noite.

Por ter brilho fraco, porém, será mais fácil encontrá-lo com binóculos ou telescópios .

A luminosidade da Lua, que estará quase cheia, também poderá dificultar a observação do planeta.

articles.title: Normal blood pressure may not tell the whole story: Scientists discover a brain ‘switch’ that could secretly raise cardiovascular risk and open new avenues for heart and brain treatments
articles.summary: An estimated 1.4 billion adults aged 30 to 79 around the world had hypertension, or high blood pressure in 2024, making it nearly 33% of the population as
articles.body: An estimated 1.4 billion adults aged 30 to 79 around the world had hypertension, or high blood pressure in 2024, making it nearly 33% of the population as per a WHO report. While, this data points towards the number of people who have been diagnosed with hypertension, and estimated 600 million adults with hypertension are not even aware. Blood pressure is a more confounding issue than meets the eye. If you've visited your doctor, no matter what problem you went approaching for, you would’ve been asked to get your blood pressure checked.Blood pressure is one of the first things we measure when we visit a doctor, and the numbers often become a quick way of understanding how well our cardiovascular system is functioning. However, what if a normal reading does not always tell us the complete story? Scientists have discovered a small group of nerve cells in the brain that helps keep blood pressure stable as the body moves between different states of activity. The discovery offers a new understanding of how the brain regulates cardiovascular health and why fluctuations in blood pressure could matter even when its average readings appear normal.The research, carried out by Scientists at the University of Virginia School of Medicine, investigates how the brain helps the body maintain steady blood pressure during everyday activities. Published in the Circulation Research journal, the study identifies a group of brainstem neurons that appear to play an important role in preventing sudden changes in blood pressure. The findings of this can eventually help researchers understand certain cardiovascular risks and develop treatments which focus not only on blood pressure levels but also on regulating themWhat happens when blood pressure appears normal?Our Blood pressure is not a fixed measurement that remains unchanged throughout the day. It naturally rises or falls as we sleep, eat, wake up or if unfortunately we find ourselves in situations that can immediately shoot this vital up. These changes are all part of our body’s response to different situations, allowing the cardiovascular system to adjust to the changing needs. However, the recent research suggests that while the average blood pressure reading may not be indicative of a heart problem, rapid or excessive changes in the blood pressure reading throughout the day can point towards a heart disease, stroke and brain injury, even if it lies in the normal range.The University of Virginia researchers have therefore investigated the neural mechanisms responsible for maintaining this balance. Their attention turned towards the brainstem, a region of the brain involved in essential automatic functions, including the regulation of breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. Within this region, the researchers studied a small population of nerve cells that play the role of maintaining steady blood pressures.These cells are located in the rostral ventrolateral medulla, an area involved in controlling the body's cardiovascular responses and researchers wanted to understand how these neurons contribute to blood pressure stability as an individual moves between different behavioural states. The findings suggest that losing even a few hundred of these cells can disrupt the mechanisms that stabilise blood pressure, causing fluctuations even when its average reading remains normal.What could this discovery mean for future treatments?The new research findings raise a possibility that disruptions in similar brain-based mechanisms could contribute to blood pressure instability in other circumstances, including situations where average readings appear normal. Understanding how these neurons work could eventually help scientists develop treatments designed to improve blood pressure stability.The health of our brain and heart is trickier to understand because the two are so deeply intertwined, as the body's responses to its environment can signal a cause for concern for both. By identifying a group of brain cells that helps maintain this delicate balance, scientists have opened another avenue for investigating how cardiovascular and neurological health intersect. However, at its current stage, the discovery remains an important step towards understanding the relationship between the brain and cardiovascular health, two aspects of our well-being that are intrinsically tied to one another.

articles.title: Common daily fiber supplement was found to significantly reduce knee pain and improve muscle strength in a new study, offering a cheap and easy option for the millions of people living with painful, stiff knees
articles.summary: Very recently, the internet was abuzz with conversations about protein and then even fibre, with the humble macronutrients taking centre stage in
articles.body: Very recently, the internet was abuzz with conversations about protein and then even fibre, with the humble macronutrients taking centre stage in discussions aboutr health and nutrition. However, the food pyramid we have all grown up studying, simple as it may appear on paper, is far more complex to follow in practice. The human body relies on an intricate network of nutrients and compounds that come together to keep the body healthy and fucntion, meaning no single fod group can meet all our meeds, but researchers wondered if a single food cannot allay all our concerns can one macronutrient be involved in helping alleviate a major one? .While joint pain is commonly associated with aging and the gradual deterioration of cartilage, researchers are increasingly investigating whether the answer to managing it could also lie somewhere beyond the joints themselves. A new clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Nottingham, published in the journal Nutrients has now discovered that a daily prebiotic fibre supplement could help alleviate knee osteoarthritis pain, improve grip strength and make the body less sensitive to painful stimuli.How a daily fibre supplement could help with knee painThe supplement which researchers focused on was inulin, a naturally occurring dietary fibre that is easily found in foods such as chicory. It is a prebiotic dietary fibre that can be beneficial for gut health, especially helpful in regular, easy digestion. Moreover, unlike nutrients that are broken down and absorbed in the small intestine, inulin passes into the large intestine, where it can be fermented by gut bacteria. It is classified as a prebiotic, meaning that it provides nourishment for certain beneficial microorganisms living in the digestive system.Dr. Afroditi Kouraki, primary author of the study from the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham notes that adding a simple fibre supplement to breakfast or yoghurt could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function. The researchers investigated whether introducing this fibre into the diet could influence knee osteoarthritis, a condition in which changes to the tissues within a joint can lead to pain, stiffness and difficulty performing everyday activities. Although existing approaches such as pain medication and physiotherapy can help manage symptoms, persistent discomfort can make regular physical activity difficult for some people.With findings that seem encouraging the trial itself was a short one, lasting only 6 weeks: the INSPIRE, a randomised clinical trial with 136 participants, out of which 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis completed the assesments. Participants were divided into four groups receiving inulin alone, digitally supported physiotherapy exercises alone, a combination of the two, or a placebo. The researchers then assessed changes in pain, physical function, muscle strength and sensitivity to painful stimuli.The results showed that both inulin supplementation and physiotherapy-supported exercise reduced knee pain compared with the placebo. However, participants receiving inulin also experienced improvements in grip strength and pain sensitivity, benefits that were not observed in the physiotherapy-only group. These findings suggest that dietary interventions may influence aspects of pain and physical function that extend beyond the affected joint.The connection between gut bacteria and pain"Our findings suggest that targeting gut health with a prebiotic supplement is a safe, well-tolerated, and effective way to reduce pain in people with knee osteoarthritis,” says Dr. Kouraki. One of the most interesting aspects of the research is the possible role played by the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract. The role of these microbes is more than just to assist in the process of digestion, as they also produce substances which interact with the body’s biological processes including effects on the pathways involved in inflammation and pain.When gut bacteria ferment inulin, they produce short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate. This compound supports the intestinal environment and is involved in biological processes that may influence inflammation. During the trial, researchers observed increased butyrate levels among participants taking inulin, pointing towards the supplement altering activity within the gut microbiome.The study also found an increase in glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a hormone released by the gut that plays a role in regulating blood sugar and appetite. Interestingly, higher GLP-1 levels were associated with better grip strength among participants. However, this association cannot determine that the hormone directly caused an improvement. Rather, it provides researchers with perhaps an explanation for how changes in the digestive system could possibly be connected to muscle function.A noteworthy observation of the study is the difference in participant retention across the treatment groups. Only 3.6 per cent of those receiving inulin alone dropped out of the study, compared with 21 per cent of those assigned to physiotherapy-supported exercise alone. This suggests that the supplement may be easier for participants to incorporate into their daily routines, although the difference in dropout rates does not establish that it is more effective than exercise.Could fibre become an additional approach for managing arthritis?The importance of this research’s findings becomes more resounding when we look at the number of people struggling with osteoarthritis pain. The findings are particularly relevant because managing osteoarthritis often requires approaches and courses of treatment that can be sustained overtime. The study conducted by the researchers offers a wonderful insight into how the alleviation of arthritis pain does not merely begin and end with the joints, but also involves a major factor: our gut health and dietary habits. While the research only nudges at possible treatment plans, health begins at home, or more precisely, in your kitchen, especially at a time when what you eat and the quantity you consume may be holding more answers than ever thought before.

articles.title: Cleopatra’s eye makeup secret? Ancient Egyptians used lead-based kohl that may have boosted the body’s immune defences and helped fight eye infections
articles.summary: Make-up as an art never began simply to enhance the appearance but to draw courage from what was not mere beauty, but power and protection.
articles.body: Make-up as an art never began simply to enhance the appearance but to draw courage from what was not mere beauty, but power and protection. Mistaken for mere garb, its long expanse across myriad empires and dynasties has symbolized unyielding power, stretched in strokes of black kohl and rosy rouge, painting a face not just to appease eyes, but to amass attention. However, National Geographic brings attention to something even more fascinating about the beauty rituals of the ancient world, especially when we discover that what people applied extended into what was believed to be medicinal.Ancient Egypt, a civilisation remembered for its elaborate jewellery, striking silhouettes and distinctive eye makeup, offers a fascinating example of how medicine and beliefs about protection could exist alongside one another. The dark, elongated eyes associated with Cleopatra, last ruling queen and pharaoh of the Ptolemaic kingdom of Egypt, has till date caught our attention. With researchers in the last few decades suggesting that certain compounds used in ancient Egyptian eye makeup could have stimulated the body’s immune defenses, a curious conversation between archaeology and modern science has now opened up.The ancient Egyptian practice of wearing kohlEye makeup was not an exclusive privilege of Egypt's queens or ruling elite. Men and women across different levels of Egyptian society wore cosmetics around their eyes, with black and green powders being among the familiar choices. Known as kohl, the dark pigment was used to define the eyes, accentuate their shape and create the distinctive appearance that continues to inspire contemporary beauty trends. Its significance, however, extended beyond aesthetics. Ancient Egyptian beliefs associated the eyes with divine protection, while cosmetics were also thought to protect the wearer against illness and the harsh conditions of the environment.The eye held considerable religious significance in Egyptian culture, with symbols such as the Eye of Horus associated with protection and well-being. Applying makeup could therefore form part of a wider understanding of personal appearance, spiritual protection and health. Historical medical texts also record the use of preparations for eye ailments, suggesting that cosmetics and remedies did not always occupy entirely separate categories in the ancient world.What scientists discovered in ancient makeupThe possible medicinal properties of Egyptian kohl attracted renewed attention when French researchers investigated its chemical composition. Their research, published in the journal Analytical Chemistry in January 2010, examined the relationship between certain lead compounds found in ancient Egyptian cosmetics and the body's response to them.Chemical analyses of ancient cosmetic samples had identified several lead-containing ingredients. Two compounds, laurionite and phosgenite, were particularly interesting because they do not occur naturally in the form used in cosmetics and appear to have been deliberately prepared. This raised questions about whether ancient Egyptian cosmetic makers understood something about the properties of the substances they were producing.The research team, including Christian Amatore and colleagues, investigated how these compounds interacted with cells. Their experiments found that very low concentrations of lead ions could stimulate skin cells, known as keratinocytes, to produce nitric oxide. This molecule plays several roles in the body, including helping regulate immune responses and contributing to defences against certain disease-causing microorganisms.The finding possibly offers an insightful explanation for why some ancient cosmetic preparations might have had a medicinal function in addition to a decorative purpose. Rather than establishing that the makeup itself prevented infections in people, however, the study demonstrated a biological response under laboratory conditions. The distinction matters because a reaction observed in cultured cells does not automatically translate into a proven health benefit when a substance is applied to the human body.Could kohl have helped protect the eyes?Eye infections would have posed a serious problem in the ancient world, and the Egyptians' use of eye preparations for health-related purposes makes the researchers' findings particularly interesting. If certain ingredients encouraged the production of nitric oxide, they might have supported some of the body's natural defences against bacteria.The researchers estimated that the quantities of the relevant compounds in the makeup could have produced a substantial increase in nitric oxide production. This led them to propose that the substances may have been intentionally prepared for their beneficial properties. However, the question of whether ancient Egyptians consciously understood the underlying chemistry remains unresolved. It is possible that generations of experience informed their practicesThe story of Egyptian eye makeup is, therefore, far more fascinating than beauty hiding a scientific secret. It takes us back thousands of years, reminding us that even something as familiar as the kohl we apply around our eyes can carry echoes of a civilisation’s beliefs, knowledge and ways of looking at the world. While we may never know whether Cleopatra’s kohl actually helped protect her eyes from infections, we certainly know that her striking eyes and the illustrious queen herself continue to leave us in awe of the beauty she once beheld.

articles.title: En 2001, un biólogo que estaba de luna de miel en Tailandia levantó una piedra en la orilla de un arroyo y descubrió el primer ciempiés gigante capaz de nadar
articles.standfirst: Ocurrió en el año 2001, pero no se dio una explicación hasta 15 años después
articles.summary: Ocurrió en el año 2001, pero no se dio una explicación hasta 15 años después
articles.body: Durante su luna de miel en Tailandia en 2001, el entomólogo George Beccaloni, del Museo de Historia Natural de Londres, levantó una piedra junto a un pequeño arroyo buscando rastros de algún animal y lo que encontró casi no podía creérselo. Debajo de esa roca encontró un extraño artrópodo de colores oscuros que se tiró directamente al agua para huir, desplazándose como si fuese una anguila. Se trataba de un ciempiés que, además, no se mojaba, ya que su coraza repelía el agua. En seguida, Beccaloni, recogió esta nueva especie y se la llevó a Londres para poder estudiarla, pero pasaron 15 años hasta que se dio una respuesta, ya que se pensaba que los ciempiés no podían nadar. Científicos de la Universidad Chulalongkorn, de Bangkok, en Tailandia, analizaron muestras procedentes de cascadas en Laos y Tailandia, además de un registro histórico de Vietnam del año 1928. Con estos datos, la especie fue bautizada en 2016 bajo el género Scolopendra. Aunque se sabe que su picadura provoca un dolor intenso, pero no mortal, el animal continúa rodeado de interrogantes. Su distribución exacta por el sudeste asiático no se conoce y los expertos no saben cuál es su dieta nocturna o sus hábitos reproductivos, ya que solo se han contabilizado cuatro individuos en todo el mundo. En declaraciones a National Geographic, George Beccaloni señaló: “Tenía un aspecto bastante terrorífico: muy grande, con patas largas y un horrible color verde negruzco oscuro. Otros Scolopendra cazan en tierra. Apostaría a que esta especie se adentra en el agua por la noche para cazar invertebrados acuáticos o anfibios”. Por su parte, Gregory Edgecombe, paleontólogo del Museo de Historia Natural de Londres, mantuvo: “Todos los Scolopendra grandes pueden propinar una picadura dolorosa; el ‘colmillo’ del sistema de inyección de veneno es capaz de atravesar nuestra piel”, sentenció.

articles.title: A Nevada manganese mine that left arsenic and lead in the ground is undergoing an estimated $257 million cleanup; a 3.5-acre park has now opened on the former site, with more than 3,000 homes planned nearby
articles.summary: What was once a mining site associated with potentially harmful industrial waste is now making way for neighbourhood parks, walking trails and thousands
articles.body: What was once a mining site associated with potentially harmful industrial waste is now making way for neighbourhood parks, walking trails and thousands of homes. In Henderson, Nevada, a former manganese mine that operated for decades and left behind contamination is being transformed into a large residential community. The opening of Greenbow Park marks a new phase in that redevelopment. According to the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (NDEP), the Three Kids Mine site has been the subject of extensive environmental assessments and a cleanup programme, with the estimated remediation cost reaching approximately $257 million.From wartime manganese production to an abandoned mining siteThe Three Kids Mine has a history dating back more than a century. Manganese ore was discovered at the site in Clark County, Nevada, in 1917. However, mining operations took place intermittently, including between 1942 and 1943 and again from 1953 to 1961. Manganese was an important industrial mineral, particularly during World War II, when demand increased for materials used in military equipment and steel production. According to the NDEP, an on-site processing mill was constructed in 1942 to meet the renewed demand for manganese during World War II. The mill reopened in 1951, and mining resumed in 1953. Mining continued until the open pits were exhausted, and operations permanently stopped in 1961.The end of mining, however, did not mean the end of the site's environmental problems. Former mine features included open pits, waste rock, an ore yard, processing facilities and tailings ponds. Environmental assessments identified dust, residues and processing waste containing lead, arsenic, manganese and petroleum. The contamination raised concerns about the condition of the land and the work needed before it could be considered suitable for redevelopment.Why the cleanup carries a $257 million price tagThe scale of the environmental work is reflected in the estimated cost. The NDEP's November 2023 Record of Decision placed the total estimated cleanup cost at approximately $257.5 million. The wider Three Kids Mine property covers around 1,165 acres, although the former mining operations affected a smaller portion of the site. The area affected by the former mining operations covered approximately 410 acres, distinguishing the contaminated mine area from the larger property earmarked for redevelopment. Environmental investigations and feasibility studies were undertaken to identify contaminants and determine the appropriate remediation measures.The federal Three Kids Mine Remediation and Reclamation Act was enacted in July 2014, creating a framework for transferring federally owned land through the City of Henderson Redevelopment Agency so that assessment, remediation and reclamation could take place. The land transfer was completed in February 2024, while major cleanup activities began in May 2024. The NDEP also established a perimeter air monitoring plan to monitor air quality during the work.The contamination identified at the site was not limited to lead and arsenic. Investigations also identified manganese, petroleum-related materials and other industrial waste. The environmental work therefore involved addressing several types of contamination rather than simply clearing away the remains of the old mine.Greenbow Park brings a new public space to the former mineOne of the most visible signs of the transformation is Greenbow Park, a new 3.5-acre recreational space that has opened on the former mine property. According to FOX5 Vegas, the park is part of the Aries master-planned community in Henderson. Its facilities include pickleball courts, playgrounds, shaded gathering areas and more than 3,000 feet of trails. Visitors can also enjoy views of the Las Vegas skyline from the walking routes.The park adds recreational space to an area being developed into a residential neighbourhood. Its opening is significant because the former industrial property is now being incorporated into a community designed around housing, outdoor activities and shared public spaces. Rather than leaving the former mining land as an isolated industrial site, the redevelopment is intended to give it a new role in Henderson's expanding urban landscape.More than 3,000 homes planned across 24 neighbourhoodsGreenbow Park is part of a much larger development plan. The Aries master-planned community is expected to include more than 3,000 homes spread across 24 residential neighbourhoods. The redevelopment covers more than 1,100 acres, making it a substantial addition to Henderson's residential growth. The community is being developed on the former Three Kids Mine property, with housing and recreational facilities planned as part of the wider project.The transformation also highlights the challenges involved in bringing previously industrial land back into urban use. Former mining properties can offer substantial redevelopment opportunities, but their conversion requires careful environmental assessment, remediation and long-term planning. There is also an important distinction between the progress of the redevelopment and the environmental project's official status. While Henderson's redevelopment director told the Las Vegas Review-Journal that remediation work had been completed, the NDEP's public project page continues to describe the overall cleanup as ongoing and lists site closure reports and monitoring documents.For Henderson, the opening of Greenbow Park offers a visible glimpse of what the former mine site could become. A property once associated with manganese production and industrial contamination is gradually taking on the appearance of a residential community, with parks, trails and thousands of homes planned as part of its next chapter.

articles.title: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman recalls Google co-founder Larry Page’s sci-fi vision from 2015 lunch at SpaceX canteen, Elon Musk says ‘he is right’
articles.summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has recounted a futuristic lunch conversation from 2015 with Google co-founder Larry Page.
articles.body: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has recounted a futuristic lunch conversation from 2015 with Google co-founder Larry Page. Revealing that the chat took place at a canteen in SpaceX, Suleyman said that Page envisioned exploring distant galaxies using advanced self-propelling probes by the end of the century. Responding to Suleyman’s story, billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk echoed the sentiment, stating that Page “might be right” in his bold prediction for human civilization.The ethics board meeting at SpaceX canteenRecalling the 2015 encounter, Suleyman said that the company chose Musk as one of the three independent members while having a conversation sitting in the canteen at SpaceX headquarters during the very first meeting of DeepMind's AI Ethics and Safety Board. When Google acquired DeepMind in 2014, Suleyman and his co-founders, Demis Hassabis and Shane Legg, made it an explicit condition of the sale that Google establish an ethics committee featuring independent oversight representation.The board structure required mutual agreement between both parties:Google executives: Larry Page, Sergey Brin, and then-Chief Legal Officer David Drummond.DeepMind co-founders: Mustafa Suleyman, Demis Hassabis, and Shane Legg.Jointly Selected Independent Board Member: Elon Musk.“Yeah, I remember in 2015 being in the canteen at SpaceX. And we had our first meeting of the Ethics and Safety Board. So when we sold DeepMind to Google, we made it a condition of our acquisition that we would have an Ethics and Safety Board with independent representation on the board,” Suleyman said in a podcast The Builders with Walter Isaacson and Kaleidoscope.“One of those independent members, because Google had to agree, which was obviously Larry, Sergey, and David Drummond at the time. And then me, Demis, and Shane had to jointly agree who those three independents would be. And so we jointly picked Elon as one of them,” he added.Suleyman noted that he remains unsure whether holding those early AI safety discussions at SpaceX headquarters played any role in influencing Musk's subsequent founding of OpenAI.“No idea if that had an influence on the founding of OpenAI or not. But so then we had our morning session and we were sitting down for lunch and I was sitting next to Larry. You know, obviously he was suspicious of me as well because he was like, you know, you’re one of those speciesists,” he recalled.Larry Page’s sci-fi vision for interstellar probesDuring lunch following the board's morning session, Suleyman found himself sitting next to Larry Page. It was during this meal that Page shared his long-term vision for deep-space exploration driven by advanced technology.“And he said, you know, I think that what you don’t understand, Mustafa, is that by the end of the century, I’m going to be exploring the galaxies at the head of a von Neumann probe,” Suleyman recalled.As Suleyman explained, a von Neumann probe is a theoretical, self-propelling robotic spacecraft designed to navigate across light-years while autonomously harvesting energy and resources directly from space.Elon Musk reacts: ‘Larry Page might be right’Revisiting the 2015 exchange, Elon Musk expressed strong support for the ambitious timeline, pointing to Page's long track record of accurate technological foresight.“Our civilization would be winning wondrously if we are exploring the galaxy with Von Neumann probes by 2100!” Musk remarked, adding, “Larry Page might be right. He has correctly predicted many things.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A two-bedroom home in Quebec was built with panels using plastic equivalent to about 200,000 discarded bottles; builders assembled its 1,078 sq ft structural shell in just three days using prefabricated parts
articles.summary: A two-bedroom home covering 1,078 sq ft in Saint-Rémi-d'Amherst, Quebec, has been built using structural panels made from the equivalent of about 200,000
articles.body: A two-bedroom home covering 1,078 sq ft in Saint-Rémi-d'Amherst, Quebec, has been built using structural panels made from the equivalent of about 200,000 recycled plastic bottles. The building shell was fully put together on-site in just three days. The project could offer a new way to build more affordable and sustainable homes across Canada. The building system, called PakVert, was developed by Quebec-based clean technology company PakVille. Founded by Canadian engineer and entrepreneur Parinaz Pakniat, the company designed prefabricated panels that combine the building structure, heat insulation, and outside finish into one lightweight part.Recycled core technologyThe centre of each PakVert panel is made from 100 per cent recycled polyethylene terephthalate (PET). This is the type of plastic commonly used in single-use drink bottles. According to technical details published by Construction Canada, the panels can be used for outside walls, floors, and roofs. They can replace several traditional building materials, including wood frames, fibreglass insulation, and outside wall panels. PakVille says the panels' dense plastic material helps protect them from moisture, mould, rot, and pests. The company also estimates that homes built with this system could last twice as long as homes built using traditional construction methods.Addressing costs and labour shortagesThe prefabricated system comes at a time when Canada's housing industry faces major challenges. Rising material costs and a shortage of workers have slowed down home construction across the country. According to PakVille, using the PakVert system can lower total construction costs by about 35 per cent compared with traditional building methods. However, the actual savings will depend on the details of each project. “People want homes they can afford, without compromising quality or comfort,” said Parinaz Pakniat, founder and chief executive officer of PakVille, in a statement reported by Construction Canada. “We developed PakVert to make construction faster, simpler, and more affordable. The fact that we're also giving plastic waste a second life makes it even more meaningful.”Assembly and energy performanceAt the construction site in Saint-Rémi-d'Amherst, workers assembled the entire 100 m2 building shell in 72 hours. Since the panels arrive ready for installation, they create much less waste on-site than traditional wood-frame construction. They also need smaller teams of workers to install. The home's owner, Daniel Massé, praised both the speed of construction and the home's ability to keep heat in after the project was completed. “When it comes to energy efficiency and speed of construction, it's a product that I would recommend to anyone,” Massé said. The project shows the growing interest in new building materials across Canada's construction industry. In particular, more attention is being given to systems that keep plastic waste out of landfills while helping build homes faster.

articles.title: Starlink Mobile is facing a major setback, as US carriers have turned down a network deal and branded satellites ‘inferior’ to existing tech
articles.summary: SpaceX will have to go it alone with Starlink Mobile, as the big three carriers have all turned down the idea of making it an MVNO.
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

T-Mobile has rejected the idea of sharing its network with Starlink

The company's CEO argues that satellite is an "inferior" technology to what T-Mobile currently uses

Verizon and AT&T have also turned Starlink down

For all its lofty ambitions, Starlink Mobile doesn't seem to be getting anywhere fast. SpaceX recently announced plans to build "the world's most advanced mobile network" using its Starlink satellites, but satellites alone won't cut it — the service also needs ground-based infrastructure and enough spectrum to power it, neither of which Starlink really has.

So its initial plan seemed to be to launch an MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) by partnering with T-Mobile, Verizon, or AT&T and gaining access to their infrastructure.

However, all three of those names have rejected SpaceX's proposition, with T-Mobile's CEO, Srini Gopalan, recently going so far as to say in an earnings call (via WCCFTech ) that "satellite is an inferior version of FWA with even more constraints in terms of things like what is the size of the beam."

FWA, or fixed wireless access, is what carriers often use to bring broadband to homes and other static locations in rural areas, combining a router with a 5G or 4G signal, rather than using fibre optic cables.

FWA exists in urban areas too, but it's particularly useful where conventional broadband struggles. So, essentially, Gopalan is arguing that satellite connectivity is a worse option, even in many rural and hard-to-reach areas, than FWA.

On top of that, Gopalan claims that "two-thirds of our FWA customers come from dense urban areas. We see huge growth opportunities in those areas still, all under the fallow capacity model. So we don't really see a synergistic opportunity with satellite providers."

All of which could be a big problem for SpaceX, as it's likely the company will have to rely primarily on its satellites for now. Though with its plans to launch 15,000 new satellites, lease 80,000 cell tower sites, and possibly install cellular base stations on existing Starlink dishes, it could still deliver a viable mobile network — and a threat to the big three — eventually.

articles.title: Satlyt takes another step toward turning satellites into space data centers  | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Satlyt ran a successful test this month bringing it closer to turning spacecraft, starting with satellites, into virtual data centers.
articles.body:
Naturally, Rama Afullo’s first reaction was, “Let’s GOOOO,” he said. His company, Satlyt , is building software to turn existing satellites into data processing networks, similar to the orbital data center concept. And he just took another step closer to that.

After 13 months of work, the company had a successful test earlier this month. Working with the University of Houston on a NASA-funded research project, the test showed how the startup’s software can spread out tasks among computers while in orbit based on communication and available compute.

He said the goal is to create software that connects to multiple satellites to share computing assignments. Users of the system “will only need to define permissions, priorities, and operating limits,” while the software will make decisions within those limits, Afullo told TechCrunch. Its software is already on three satellites in orbit and the first step to that vision was this test. While the test used NASA-funded research, the agency has not yet selected it for any particular mission or chosen it to deploy its technology.

Afullo said NASA missions face the same constraints that Satlyt hopes to address — “limited computing resources, intermittent communication, and the need to get useful information back to people.”

In this test, the company created a simulated network with four computers, four users, and eight services. The software then assessed how to assign and run tasks on those computers, accounting for compute and communication availability. One physical computer aboard a spacecraft ran the experiment, evaluating a simulated network of four computing hosts, then returned the results to Earth. The test proved that Satlyt’s software can generate plans on hardware in orbit, but more testing will be done to see how those computers transfer information amongst each other in practice when multiple physical computers are used.

“The finding is a trade-off,” he said. One approach worked best, though it required more computing power than the others.

Still, Satlyt which was in the top five of TechCrunch Disrupt Battlefield this year, calls this a win. “It’s a building block toward satellites sharing computing work,” he said.

NASA already has a technology network designed to move data through space even when communication links face delays. It started using this tech earlier this year and has already tested it on aircraft.

Afullo, who previously worked at Google and SpaceX, founded Satlyt in 2024 to turn spacecraft into virtual data centers. Its software helps operators run AI and other applications onboard, processing data closer to where it is collected and reducing dependence on downlinks, where satellites send data back to Earth, and ground-based analysis.

For example, if a spacecraft sees a wildfire on Earth, such software can help it transmit relevant information much faster. “The goal is to get useful answers to people sooner and make better use of limited communication windows,” he said. “This experiment tested one planning component of that broader capability.”

Satlyt said it still needs to test its own software under various workloads, hardware, and connectivity conditions. They also found an issue in how their software was time-referencing delays, Afullo said — it was stamping it as arrival time (the time it arrived) rather than elapsed delay (how long it took to arrive), which is a different metric.

It doesn’t mean the experiment failed, however. “The software development, onboard execution, and return of outputs succeeded,” he said.

But Afullo said much work remains. “We also need usable communication links, permission from participating operators, secure transfers, resource scheduling, and recovery when a connection of computers becomes unavailable.” Satlyt is also researching applications beyond low Earth orbit, including supporting 4K video streaming from the Moon through its NASA-funded work.

“Our next technical steps are broader validation and integration, followed by demonstrations of computing work shared across separate spacecraft,” he said. “Longer term, we want developers to build applications for space without having to rebuild the infrastructure for every mission. That’s what virtual AI data centers in space mean to us.”

articles.body: Google’s AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. articles.title: In 2025, scientists examined three king cobra encounters in Thailand, revealing a little-known side of the venomous snakes that had long been missing from scientific research
articles.summary: Two male king cobras meeting during the breeding season may engage in a prolonged contest, using their bodies to wrestle for control rather than relying
articles.body: Two male king cobras meeting during the breeding season may engage in a prolonged contest, using their bodies to wrestle for control rather than relying on the venomous strikes associated with these snakes. The behaviour has long been recognised in accounts of king cobras, yet detailed scientific descriptions have been scarce. In Thailand, observations made during the 2019 breeding season provided researchers with an opportunity to examine these encounters more closely. A paper published in 2025 documented three instances of ritual combat involving the northern king cobra, adding direct and indirect evidence to a part of the species' natural history that had largely rested on anecdotal reports.King cobra combat study documents three encounters in Thailand during 2019According to the Ecology and Evolution study, titled 'Ritualistic male–male combat of the northern king cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) in Thailand', published by David Roman Bontrager and colleagues. The team recorded three instances of combat during the 2019 breeding season in Thailand, drawing on both direct observations and indirect evidence.The distinction matters because the behaviour is familiar to people who study snakes, but its details have not been well documented in published research on king cobras. Accounts and footage shared informally have suggested that males engage in physical contests, yet they do not always provide enough information to describe what happens, how the encounter develops or how it ends.The researchers set out to record these events in a scientific account. Their work adds observations of northern king cobras to the literature on ritualised combat, a behaviour also known in several other snake species.What happens when male snakes competeRitual combat in snakes generally involves two males attempting to overpower one another through physical contact. The contest can include raising the front portion of the body, pressing against an opponent and attempting to force the other snake down. Unlike a straightforward attack on prey, the interaction is primarily a contest between rivals.Such encounters are associated with competition for access to mates. A male that succeeds in forcing its opponent into a subordinate position may gain an advantage during the breeding season. The outcome does not necessarily depend on which snake is larger, since strength, positioning and the ability to maintain control can all influence the contest.King cobras are among the world's largest venomous snakes, and their size makes these encounters particularly striking. Their reputation for venomous bites can also obscure the difference between a defensive or predatory interaction and a contest between males. Ritual combat is a separate form of behaviour, in which physical dominance rather than the delivery of venom is central.Why the king cobra's changing classification mattersThe research also comes after a major change in how scientists classify king cobras. The animals once treated as a single widespread species have been divided into four distinct species within the king cobra complex. Behaviour reported in one population cannot automatically be assumed to apply in the same way to every member of the group. Differences in habitat, breeding patterns and other aspects of natural history may emerge as scientists gather more evidence from the newly recognised species.The northern king cobra, Ophiophagus hannah, is the focus of the Thai observations described in the paper. By identifying the animals within the revised classification, the authors help establish which species the recorded behaviour applies to, rather than treating the findings as evidence for all king cobras without qualification.How three king cobra encounters help fill a gap in scientific researchThe authors point to a gap between the accepted understanding of king cobra behaviour and the published evidence supporting it. Male–male combat has commonly been regarded as part of the species' natural history, but detailed descriptions of the interactions have been missing from the primary literature.Observations shared by field workers and members of the public have helped establish that such contests occur. The problem is that informal accounts can vary in the information they provide, making it difficult to compare events or draw firm conclusions about how the behaviour works.By bringing three encounters into a scientific paper, the researchers provide a starting point for further comparisons. The observations can be considered alongside reports of ritual combat in other snakes, helping scientists examine which features may be shared across species and which might be specific to king cobras.What the observations add to king cobra researchKing cobras are difficult animals to study in the wild. They occupy a range of habitats across parts of Asia, and their size, behaviour and venom make close observation challenging. As a result, some aspects of their lives are better known than others. Their feeding habits and defensive displays have received attention, while specific interactions between breeding adults have been less thoroughly recorded.The Thailand paper adds detail to that less-documented area. Its three observations do not provide a complete account of the species' mating behaviour, but they give researchers material that can be examined, compared and tested against future field records.

articles.title: Scientists covered part of a Chinese glacier with fabric to slow melting; ice loss fell by 27% initially, but the effect weakened
articles.summary: A layer of artificial fabric reduced melting on a section of China’s Dagu Glacier by 15% over one year, as per the study.
articles.body: A layer of artificial fabric reduced melting on a section of China’s Dagu Glacier by 15% over one year, as per the study. Researchers covered about 500 square metres of Dagu Glacier No. 17 with non-woven geotextile in August 2020 and monitored changes in the ice through October 2021.According to the research published in Remote Sensing, titled ‘Applying Artificial Cover to Reduce Melting in Dagu Glacier in the Eastern Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau’, the covered area lost less ice than nearby uncovered sections, although the material became less effective over time. During the first two months, melting was reduced by 27%. In a later two-month comparison, the reduction was 8%. The researchers linked the decline partly to a fall in the fabric’s ability to reflect sunlight and said cost and difficult access limited wider use on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau.Researchers installed a 500-square-metre fabric cover on Dagu GlacierResearchers installed the geotextile on 5 August 2020 along the glacier’s main flowline, about 50 metres from its terminus. The covered patch measured 500 square metres, equivalent to around 1% of the glacier’s total area. The team chose non-woven geotextile made from synthetic fibres because earlier research had found that this material offered strong insulation performance.The fabric was carried by gondola to an altitude of about 4,800 metres, then taken to the site by workers. Researchers secured the rolls together and fixed them in place with ropes and bags containing stones. They compared the covered ice with nearby uncovered areas using field measurements, terrestrial laser scanning and drone surveys.Fabric cover reduced Dagu Glacier’s melting by 27% in two monthsThe difference between the covered and uncovered ice became clear within two months. By 17 October 2020, the covered surface stood an average of 0.46 metres higher than the surrounding uncovered surface. Measurements showed that the uncovered area melted at 1.9 centimetres per day, compared with 1.2 centimetres per day beneath the fabric. The researchers calculated that the cover reduced melting by 27% during this period and preserved about 178 cubic metres of ice. These results showed that the fabric had slowed ice loss during the initial observation period overall.Dagu Glacier cover reduced annual melting by 15%Monitoring over the following year found that the fabric continued to limit melting, but the difference narrowed. Terrestrial laser scans comparing October 2020 with October 2021 showed an average surface elevation change of 2.7 metres in uncovered areas and 2.3 metres in the protected section.The researchers calculated an annual reduction in melting of 15%. Drone surveys also compared changes between August and October 2021. During those two months, the covered area lost an average of 1.1 metres in elevation, while the uncovered area lost 1.2 metres. This represented an 8% reduction in melting, compared with the 27% reduction recorded in the first two months after installation during the study.Glacier blanket loses reflectivity over timeThe researchers measured a decline in the fabric’s albedo, or ability to reflect sunlight, from 0.71 in October 2020 to 0.39 in October 2021. They said this reduced reflectivity meant the material absorbed more solar energy and became less effective at protecting the ice.Deposited impurities and staining may also have contributed, while low temperatures and humidity could cause the fabric to crack. The study said these effects of ageing needed further investigation. The researchers also highlighted practical limits: high costs, difficult access to high-altitude glaciers, and the challenge of removing fabric that freezes to the ice.

articles.title: Meet Locklyn Raye Ward, the Oklahoma eighth-grader who tested 24 wild plants from her family's farm and found 56% showed antibacterial activity, though none beat antibiotics
articles.summary: Locklyn Raye Ward, an Oklahoma eighth-grader, worked on a study titled, “A Study of Open Field Plants, Native and Non-Native, and Their Antimicrobial
articles.body: Locklyn Raye Ward, an Oklahoma eighth-grader, worked on a study titled, “A Study of Open Field Plants, Native and Non-Native, and Their Antimicrobial Properties Against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus epidermidis.” Details about Locklyn’s project and background come from the Society for Science, the nonprofit behind Science News and several student science competitions. It all started with what she thought were weeds. One evening, Locklyn was feeding cows on the farm when she and her dad drove past some plants she thought were weeds. He told her it was pokeweed, growing wild. “He said he had always heard it was healthy in many ways,” she says. She was already worried about the overuse of antibiotics. So she started to wonder if other wild plants on the farm might have antibiotic properties and how those would compare with the antibiotics used in medicine. Locklyn picked 24 plants, and 12 of them were native to Oklahoma. She weighed each plant, cut it into one-gram pieces, and boiled it in distilled water to pull out any chemicals inside.Next, she grew Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus epidermidis on agar plates. She soaked small paper discs in the plant extracts and dropped them onto the plates. Where an extract held antibiotic compounds, the bacteria around the disc would die. For comparison, she tested discs covered in commercial antibiotics too, and she measured how many bacteria each extract or antibiotic could kill. After 24 hours of incubation, 56 per cent of the plants showed some antibacterial properties. Seven of the native plants were active. None of them worked as well as the commercial antibiotics.How did she test the plants?Locklyn picked 24 different plants. Twelve were native to Oklahoma, and twelve were not. She weighed the plants, cut them into one-gram pieces, and boiled the pieces in distilled water to pull out any chemicals they might contain.Next came the bacteria. She grew Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus epidermidis on agar plates. Then she soaked small paper discs in her plant extracts and dropped them onto the plates. The idea was simple: if an extract held antibiotic compounds, the bacteria around its disc would die.To have something to measure against, Locklyn also got discs covered in commercial antibiotics and tested them alongside the plant extracts. For each extract and each antibiotic, she measured how many bacteria it could kill. Then the plates sat for 24 hours of incubation.When the time was up, she counted the results. Of the plants she collected, 56 per cent showed some antibacterial properties. Seven of the native plants showed antibiotic activity. None of them, though, were as effective as commercial antibiotics.What did the results say?Locklyn began with two questions. Did the wild plants on her farm have any antibiotic properties, and how did those properties compare with antibiotics used in medicine? The plates gave her two answers. More than half of the plants she collected did show some activity, and seven of the 12 native plants were among them. But in every case, the commercial antibiotics did better.The second answer matters as much as the first. Because she tested the plants next to commercial antibiotics, she could see where they actually stood instead of only noticing that something had happened around a disc. Her dad had always heard that pokeweed was healthy in many ways. Locklyn took that kind of passed-along idea and put it through a measured test, with a clear standard to compare against.Beyond the projectLocklyn is active in her church and enjoys church activities the most. "I attend a very old church in the country. Walking into this building gives me an instant peaceful feeling," she says. "I can gather my thoughts and fears in peace and quiet. After Sunday, I am ready to tackle the problems and issues of the upcoming week."In the summer, she attends church camps and basketball camps. She has also volunteered at basketball camps with elementary school kids, passing on her skills to younger players. Locklyn helps on her family's farm as well, which is the same place where her project began.Locklyn's project began with a few plants she mistook for weeds. It ended with 24 plants tested, two kinds of bacteria, a set of commercial antibiotics for comparison and a clear result. Some of the plants growing wild on her family's farm showed antibiotic activity, and none of them beat the medicines. For a student worried about antibiotic overuse, that is a real answer to a real question.

articles.title: Scientists put brown anoles on 3 artificial Florida islands; within 3 months native green anoles climbed higher, then evolved larger, stickier toe pads
articles.summary: A recent study published in Science highlights how native green anoles evolved larger, stickier toe pads and changed their perch behavior within months of brown anole invasion on artificial Florida islands.
articles.body: In the 1990s, when Cuban brown anoles were introduced to three small artificial islands off Florida’s eastern coast, the native green anoles who were already living there began changing where they perched. In just three months, the green lizards were found already climbing higher into the trees, away from the lower areas which were increasingly occupied by the newly introduced animals. Over the next 15 years, researchers noted a second change: green anole populations living alongside the invader had evolved larger toe pads with more adhesive scales, which are traits associated with a stronger grip on narrow branches. Published in the journal Science in October 2014, the findings made way for a rare opportunity to observe behavioural change followed by measurable evolutionary adaptation in a native species.Three islands received the invasive lizardsThe research centred around two closely related species: the native green anole (Anolis carolinensis) and the Cuban brown anole (Anolis sagrei), which is native to the Bahamas and Cuba. While green anoles are common across the southeastern United States, brown anoles have spread through parts of the region after being introduced. Both species overlap in their use of habitat and food resources, thus creating opportunities for competition when they occupy the same area.Yoel Stuart, an evolutionary biologist, alongside his colleagues, used six small islands in Florida’s Intracoastal Waterway to examine the outcomes when the two species shared the same habitat. The islands were man-made, formed from material dredged during earlier construction work. Researchers introduced brown anoles to three islands of different sizes and left three similarly sized islands without any invaders. This arrangement of the experiment allowed the team to compare changes in the native lizard’s behaviour between locations that are invaded and uninvaded.The team had expected a competition for food and space to influence how the native lizards used their habitat. The possibility of predation on hatchlings also played a role, as adults of either species could eat the young of the other. Therefore, moving higher into the trees could reduce encounters with brown anoles that generally occupied lower perches. These interactions were considered by the researchers as pressures behind the native lizards’ change in habitat use, instead of establishing a single mechanism as the sole cause.Green anoles changed their behaviour within three monthsThe shift was noticed quickly. The brown anoles were introduced in May 1995, and by August the same year, green anoles on the three experimental islands were already perching relatively higher than those on control islands. With continued monitoring, the researchers documented that the difference in perch height persisted.Higher branches, meanwhile, presented different physical challenges. They were usually thinner, smoother and less stable than the lower perches the lizards had previously used. Therefore, holding onto these surfaces required a better grip. In anoles, that ability is associated with the size of the toe pads and the number of lamellae, which are specialised scales on their undersides. These scales carry microscopic hair-like structures known as setae, which help the lizards to cling to surfaces.Larger toe pads emerged over generationsSubsequently, researchers returned to the islands to check if the behavioural shift was accompanied by physical changes. In 2010, they compared green anoles from islands where brown anoles were introduced with populations on islands that remained uninvaded. The native lizards living alongside the introduced species showed larger toe pads and more lamellae. These traits are associated with improved clinging ability on narrow and smooth perches.The crew estimated that this divergence had developed over approximately 15 years, or around 20 generations. This implied that measurable evolutionary differences could emerge over a relatively short period when populations faced sustained ecological pressures.To analyse whether the toe-pad differences were just caused by individual lizards growing up on higher branches, the team opted to conduct a common-garden experiment in 2011. They collected gravid green anole females from invaded and uninvaded islands, gathered their eggs and raised them under identical laboratory conditions. The offspring retained the toe-pad characteristics similar to those observed in their respective parental populations. These supported the hypothesis that the differences had a genetic basis; researchers even acknowledged that secondary transgenerational plastic factors deserved further study.

articles.title: Why are US, Russia and China racing to put nuclear reactors on the moon?
articles.summary: Reactors could revolutionise moon exploration, providing energy for bases and mining, but risks of contamination remain.
articles.body:
The United States, Russia and China are racing to build nuclear reactors on the moon, as scientists warn about the possible risk of a radioactive mishap.

In January, NASA, the US space agency, announced plans to develop a nuclear reactor on the moon by the end of 2030. Russia, working with China, aims to do the same by 2036 as they strive to advance space exploration.

The reactors will be needed to power mining of frozen water trapped deep in the moon’s craters, which scientists believe could supply drinking water, air, and rocket fuel for future bases. The reactors would also provide power for lunar bases.

Which countries want to put nuclear reactors on the moon?

The US said NASA’s Lunar Reactor 1 would produce 20 kilowatts of electricity, creating enough power to run on its own for five years without maintenance.

NASA’s reactor is designed to be compact, weighing under 6,000kg (13,200 lbs) and will fit inside a rocket compartment measuring 3.7 metres (12 feet) long by 5.5 metres (18 ft) wide.

Russia is also building a nuclear reactor, which is expected to produce 10 kilowatts. The reactor, called Selena, will be able to run for a decade without maintenance. It will be ready to power a Chinese-led moon base by about 2036.

The Selena reactor is expected to be even lighter than NASA’s, weighing about 1,100 to 1,300kg (2,400 to 2,800 lbs) for an easier and softer landing on the lunar surface.

This would not be the first time nuclear reactors have been placed in outer space.

The Soviet Union launched more than 30 nuclear fission reactors into Earth’s orbit between the late 1960s and the 1980s to power spy satellites during the Cold War.

The small, 1,000kg (2,200 lbs) reactors powered radar-tracking spy satellites using heat from splitting uranium atoms into 3 to 5 kilowatts of electricity. They are no longer operational, and no other country has sent nuclear reactors into space.

The US has spent $20bn on advanced space nuclear programmes over the past 70 years, but has never successfully launched a nuclear reactor into space since an experiment in 1965.

That experiment was carried out to see if nuclear energy could power a satellite. It worked at first but accidentally shut down after just 43 days because a non-nuclear electrical part of the satellite broke down. It is still floating up in space today.

Previous attempts by the US to develop nuclear projects have stalled due to shifting budget priorities .

How do you put nuclear reactors on the moon?

First, scientists will have to build a reactor on Earth, which will then be transported to the moon using a robotic spacecraft that fires rocket engines for a slow and gentle touchdown.

Both the US and Russia say they would keep their reactors switched off until they reach the moon, to keep radioactive risk at a minimum until the last step.

Once set up on the moon, the reactors would be designed to run without maintenance for years, supplying power to bases engaged in mining on the lunar surface.

Why does the moon need a nuclear reactor?

The US, China and Russia want to build bases near the moon’s south pole, close to the known sources of water ice. The ice sits in the permanently shadowed craters, where sunlight has not reached for millions of years.

As well as powering the moon bases, the reactors would also supply enough power for mining. So far, the US, Russia and China want to mine for frozen water which, once released, could be used to support life on the moon at bases where people could live and conduct research.

Tech billionaire Elon Musk has also said he wants to extract minerals such as aluminium, titanium, and silicon, required for manufacturing satellites.

Solar power for such endeavours would be limited as the sun shines on any one spot on the moon only half the time, so solar panels would go dark for about two weeks every month.

Simon Middleburgh, director of Bangor University’s Nuclear Futures Institute (NFI), told Al Jazeera that solar power is too limited to provide the steady flow of energy a moon base would need, while batteries and diesel are too costly, because everything has to be launched from Earth.

Nuclear energy is the “obvious choice”, Middleburgh said, adding that it must be used “responsibly”.

It is likely that three or four reactors working together would be required to provide sufficient energy for mining lunar ice as well as supporting a moon base, he added.

In a December 2025 executive order , US President Donald Trump ordered NASA to build a lunar reactor ready to launch by 2030. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin have revealed similar plans.

In August this year, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said the US is in a “race to the moon, in a race with China”.

Middleburgh said the 2030 deadline is likely for building the reactor itself, but the harder part will be landing on the moon and safely setting up the system.

“The biggest challenge isn’t really the nuclear technology at all; it is the regulation for launch, the availability of a launch platform itself, and the landing and setting up the system on the lunar surface ready for it to be operated sustainably and safely,” he said.

The race to the moon also comes amid growing military competition beyond Earth. In September, the US announced it had deployed weapons into orbit , which officials said would be used to defend US forces.

While the US did not provide details about these “weapons”, experts say they are likely to be space-based communications jammers, rather than kinetic ones that launch strikes.

The announcement raised concerns about the concept of “space weapons” or the use of space for military purposes, including the potential targeting of satellites that provide GPS, communications and intelligence.

Middleburgh told Al Jazeera that an accident during the launch of the reactors would be less frightening than it sounds because uranium alone, before it is used in a reactor, is not very radioactive. However, that changes once the reactor is switched on.

The risk is bigger if a running reactor falls back onto Earth, analysts say.

In 1978, a Soviet satellite carrying a reactor, Kosmos 954, scattered radioactive material across nearly 124,300 square km (48,000sq miles) of northern Canada.

The accident forced an expensive military cleanup of the highly radioactive fragments and microscopic particles.

On the moon, Middleburgh says, any contaminated area would be “extremely localised” if there were to be a similar accident.

Legally, no one. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans countries from “claiming” the moon or any part of it, though they have ownership of the equipment they send there. The treaty does not ban nuclear power in space.

Antonino Salmeri, director of the Lunar Policy Platform, a nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that a reactor can be lawful if it follows the treaty’s principles, including peaceful use and avoiding harmful contamination.

Norbert Schorghofer, a senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute in Arizona, US, told Al Jazeera all signatories “have the right to mine the lunar surface as long as it is for peaceful purposes”.

Whichever country’s reactor gets to the “best” water ice first could claim a “safety zone”, which would not be a land claim but could operate like one. Salmeri said declaring one creates no territorial rights, but a reactor shuts others out anyway, because nobody wants to enter a radioactive area.

A Lunar Policy Platform report released last month points to another problem: Who is responsible if something goes wrong? The report says existing liability rules have not been designed to regulate the use of long-term hazardous equipment on another celestial body.
